title: MDCAT Chemistry: Organic vs Inorganic — Where to Focus
excerpt: Chemistry splits into Physical, Organic, and Inorganic — and each one demands a different kind of studying. Here's how to divide your time instead of treating all three the same way.

content.text: Chemistry isn't one subject — it's three

A lot of MDCAT study plans treat "Chemistry" as a single block of hours on a timetable. That undersells how different Physical, Organic, and Inorganic Chemistry actually are to study. One rewards numerical practice, one rewards mechanism logic, and one rewards structured memorization. Studying all three the same way — rereading notes, for instance — plays to the strengths of only one of them.

Confirm the exact chapter list and current subtopic depth for each of the three sections against the official PMDC MDCAT syllabus. This post focuses on how to study each type of content, not on exact per-section mark counts, since those vary by source and by test cycle.
Organic Chemistry: the one that eats the most time

Across MDCAT prep resources, Organic Chemistry is consistently flagged as the section that typically carries the most weight within Chemistry — and it's also the section students most often say feels overwhelming, because it isn't really memorization or calculation. It's both, layered together: you need to know structures, name reactions, follow mechanisms, and recognize functional group transformations, often several steps removed from the original compound.
The chapters usually involved include:

items: Reaction mechanisms and functional group interconversions

content.text: The mistake students make here is treating Organic like an Inorganic-style memorization task — trying to memorize each reaction as an isolated fact. It works much better to understand the underlying pattern (why a particular mechanism happens, not just that it happens), because MDCAT questions frequently test a reaction you haven't seen before applied to a new compound, using the same underlying principle.
Inorganic Chemistry: less time-intensive, but unforgiving on detail

Inorganic Chemistry tends to be the most straightforwardly memory-based of the three sections — periodic trends, properties of elements and compounds across the s-block, p-block, and d-block, and specific reactions or exceptions that don't always follow the "expected" pattern. There's comparatively less conceptual complexity than Organic, but the volume of specific facts is large, and MDCAT questions here often hinge on catching an exception rather than the general rule.

This is the section where comparison tables tend to help more than linear notes — periodic trends, in particular, are much easier to retain when you can see how one element's properties shift against its neighbors, rather than reading about each element as a standalone paragraph.
Physical Chemistry: numerical, but formulaic once you know the pattern

Physical Chemistry — mole concept, gas laws, chemical equilibrium, thermochemistry, electrochemistry, reaction kinetics — is arguably the most "learnable" of the three sections in a short amount of time, because it's rule-based rather than memory-based. Once you understand a formula and the situations where it applies, most of the difficulty is in speed and accuracy under exam pressure, not in recalling new information.

MDCAT numericals are typically solved without a calculator, so timed practice matters more here than in Organic or Inorganic — the goal isn't just knowing the formula, it's applying it quickly enough within the time you have per question.

Because Physical Chemistry rewards repetition more directly than the other two sections, it's often the fastest place to see measurable improvement if you're running short on time before the exam — a week of focused numerical practice tends to move your Physical Chemistry accuracy more than a week of rereading Organic mechanisms moves your Organic accuracy.
Where students misallocate their time

The most common pattern worth avoiding: spending a disproportionate share of Chemistry study time re-reading Organic notes because it feels the least secure, while Inorganic gets treated as "I'll memorize it closer to the exam" and Physical Chemistry numericals get delayed because they feel solvable "whenever."
In practice, all three need dedicated time on a different schedule:

items: Organic benefits from steady, spaced-out practice over weeks, since mechanism recognition builds slowly
Inorganic benefits from active recall closer to the exam, since it's more about fresh memory than deep understanding
Physical Chemistry benefits from frequent short numerical practice sessions throughout your prep, not just a single cram session

content.text: Building a realistic Chemistry study split

If you're deciding how to divide a week of Chemistry study time, a reasonable default is to give Organic the largest single share — given how consistently it's flagged as the heaviest section — while making sure Physical Chemistry gets frequent shorter sessions rather than being pushed to "whenever there's time left." Inorganic can be scheduled in blocks that get revisited on a rotation, since it holds up well under spaced repetition without needing daily attention.

If you want a sense of how your Chemistry preparation is tracking against the aggregate you'll need for a specific college, our merit calculator can give you a starting estimate to work from as your prep continues.
The bottom line

Organic, Inorganic, and Physical Chemistry aren't interchangeable study blocks — they ask for different kinds of effort and reward different study habits. Organic rewards understanding the pattern behind a mechanism, not memorizing it in isolation. Inorganic rewards structured, comparison-based memorization closer to the exam. Physical Chemistry rewards frequent numerical practice under time pressure. Matching your study method to each section, instead of applying one approach across all of Chemistry, is usually a bigger lever than adding more raw hours.

items.question: Which part of MDCAT Chemistry carries the most weight — Organic, Inorganic, or Physical?
items.answer: Organic Chemistry is consistently flagged across MDCAT prep resources as the section that typically carries the most weight within Chemistry, though exact percentages vary by source — confirm against the official PMDC syllabus.

items.question: How should I study Organic Chemistry differently from Inorganic?
items.answer: Organic rewards understanding the underlying pattern behind a mechanism rather than memorizing each reaction as an isolated fact, since MDCAT often tests unfamiliar reactions using the same principle. Inorganic is more straightforwardly memory-based and benefits from comparison tables and active recall closer to the exam.

items.question: Is a calculator allowed for MDCAT Physical Chemistry numericals?
items.answer: No — MDCAT numericals are typically solved without a calculator, which makes timed practice especially important here, since the goal is applying formulas quickly under time pressure, not just knowing them.

items.question: Which Chemistry section improves fastest with focused practice?
items.answer: Physical Chemistry tends to show the fastest measurable improvement, since it's rule-based rather than memory-based — a week of focused numerical practice typically moves accuracy more than the same time spent rereading Organic mechanisms.

items.question: How should I schedule my Chemistry study time across the three sections?
items.answer: Give Organic steady, spaced-out practice over weeks since mechanism recognition builds slowly, revisit Inorganic in rotating blocks closer to the exam since it holds up well under spaced repetition, and give Physical Chemistry frequent short numerical sessions throughout your prep rather than a single cram session.
